notes.meaning: God gave directions to build the main altar for animal sacrifices, which stood in the open courtyard in front of the tent. It was square, measuring about seven and a half feet on each side and four and a half feet high. This height made it easy for priests to tend the fire and arrange the offerings while standing on the ground.

differ.view: The bronze altar points directly to Christ Himself, whose divine nature supported the sacrifice of His human nature, rather than picturing the cross or the Lord's Table.
The altar represents the cross as the place of death where Jesus made atonement and where believers must put self to death.

notes.meaning: Horn-shaped points were carved directly onto each of the four top corners, and the whole wooden frame was plated with bronze to protect it from heat. Sacrificial animals were tied to these horns, and priests smeared blood on them during ceremonies of atonement (being cleansed from sin). They also served as a place of refuge where someone accused of a crime could hold on and plead for mercy.

All the tools used at the altar were cast from bronze so they could endure heavy work and intense heat. Pots held the fat-soaked ashes, shovels cleared them away, and bowls caught the blood of the animals for sprinkling. Meat forks were used to turn the offerings on the fire, while pans carried burning coals across to the incense altar inside the tent.

A bronze metal grating was placed inside the altar, hanging halfway down like a sturdy net. This grate held the burning wood and meat, allowing air to fan the flames while ashes dropped through to the bottom. Rings were fixed to its corners so the entire grate could be lifted and transported when the camp moved.

Carrying poles were carved from acacia wood and overlaid with bronze, matching the altar itself. When the Israelites broke camp to travel, these poles slid through rings on the sides. This allowed the priests to carry the holy altar on their shoulders without touching the sacred frame directly.

The altar was constructed as a hollow wooden box rather than a solid block, making it light enough to carry through the desert. Moses was reminded to follow the exact pattern God had shown him on Mount Sinai. Worship had to follow God's design rather than human invention.

differ.view: The altar was kept completely hollow as a picture of Christ emptying Himself when He became human, rejecting the idea that it was ever filled with earth.

notes.meaning: God commanded a large rectangular courtyard to surround the tabernacle, marking it off from the rest of the camp. The south wall was about one hundred and fifty feet long and made of fine white linen curtains hung from posts. This enclosure provided a sacred, open-air space where ordinary Israelites could gather to pray and bring their offerings.

Both the south and north sides were supported by twenty posts resting in sturdy bronze bases. Silver hooks and silver connecting rods held the linen curtains smoothly in place. The silver added beauty to the sacred boundary, while the bronze bases kept the wooden pillars anchored firmly against desert winds.

The back of the courtyard on the west side and the front on the east side were each fifty cubits wide, or about seventy-five feet across. Ten posts with bronze bases held up the western wall behind the tabernacle. The eastern wall faced the rising sun and contained the only entrance into the sacred grounds.

On the east side, the wall was split to make room for a wide gateway in the center. Linen curtains stretched twenty-two and a half feet on the left side and the same distance on the right side. Each of these side sections was supported by three posts set into bronze bases.

The gate itself was a wide opening of thirty feet, covered by a curtain woven with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn alongside fine linen. These rich colors matched the entrance to the tabernacle tent, clearly showing worshipers where to enter. It hung on four posts with bronze bases, offering an inviting and beautiful way into God's presence.

All the pillars around the courtyard were united by silver rods, fitted with silver hooks, and set into bronze bases. The whole courtyard measured about one hundred and fifty feet long, seventy-five feet wide, and seven and a half feet high. Because the linen wall was only half the height of the tabernacle tent, the sacred building could still be seen rising above it from outside.

Every tool used for setting up, taking down, and maintaining the tabernacle was made of bronze, along with the tent pegs for the structure and the courtyard. Bronze was durable enough to withstand hard use and being driven into stony ground. These pegs and cords kept the tall posts and curtains stable against the wilderness winds.

The Israelites were commanded to supply the finest olive oil to keep the golden lampstand burning. This was beaten oil, gently crushed in a mortar rather than pressed in a heavy mill, giving a clean flame free of dark smoke and soot. It reminded the people that God's house was to be filled with pure and constant light.

The golden lampstand stood in the Holy Place, right in front of the inner curtain that hid the Ark of the Covenant. Aaron and his sons were responsible for trimming the wicks and refilling the oil every evening so the light shone all night before the Lord. This daily duty was a lasting law for Israel, reminding them of God's continual, watchful presence among them.

differ.view: The command to keep the lamps burning continually meant they were tended so they burned faithfully day and night without ever going out.
The phrase continually meant the lamps were lit every evening and put out each morning, since the tabernacle had natural daylight through the front curtain.
